legend.summary: Lightning seen from the International Space Station from March 2017 to July 2023, in 14 equal parts, in order. A scan line crosses the world once per part, west to east.
legend.method: The sound moves with the scan line: from your left ear at the western edge of the map, through the centre, to your right ear at the eastern edge. North sounds higher and south lower. Listen to the storms swing north and south and back again as the seasons turn, about seven times. To hear what changed instead, turn on Compare with previous part (key C): each sweep then plays the difference between this part and the one before it, in the same places.

items.meaning: Lightning marks in NASA's movie, each played as the scan line crosses it. A lone mark is one quiet note; many marks together make a soft, quick flurry. Higher = farther north.
How many lightning marks are close to the scan line. It swells over busy storms and dies away over calm places.
How much of the map under the scan line is lit by lightning. It never stops, and stays in the middle.
Where the storms are, north or south, moment by moment. Every stretch of latitude has its own string note, higher = farther north, and it swells while lightning there is under the scan line.
More lightning here than in the previous part. A bigger increase is louder and climbs further.
Less lightning here than in the previous part. Places that stayed the same are quiet.

legend.caveat: Values are read from the colours of NASA's video, not from the satellite measurements, so they are relative. A mark is a yellow dot in the movie, counted once when it first appears; it is not a measured flash, and in the busiest storms dots land on top of each other, so counts there are too low. The sensor sees only from about 55 degrees north to 55 degrees south. NASA's movie has no dates, so the parts are equal stretches of the movie, not calendar months. The movie runs at an uneven speed, so parts hold different spans of time, and the number of marks in a part depends on that too; the last part includes the movie's ending, where no new marks appear. Compare mode uses how much of the map is lit, which does not depend on the speed.

frames.alt: World map of lightning, part 1 of 14 of NASA's record from March 2017 to July 2023: yellow where lightning was seen, on both sides of the equator.
frames.text: Part 1 of 14. Lightning in this part of NASA's record: 63 percent of the busiest part, on both sides of the equator. About 33,000 separate lightning marks appear in NASA's movie during this part. Most lightning: around Kinshasa, around Kananga and around Dallas.
